Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

imagination noun

also imaginative, use your imagination, in your imagination, fantasy

classical

Auct. Her. 3.32: cōgitātiō enim quamvīs regiōnem potest amplectī (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Tusc. 1.50: cōgitātiōne comprehendere (Lewis & Short)

cōgitātiō, cōgitātiōnis f.

noun, third declension

thought, the mind’s power of picturing

Classical prose has no single word for the faculty; it says “thought” and “the mind”: cōgitātiōne fingere, animō fingere (see imagine). Its everyday sense is simply thinking or a thought.

Other words

  • ingenium, ingeniī n. — inventiveness, natural talent

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · M-O s.v. imagination: creativity (inventiō)

    Imagination as the gift of invention: a person’s natural cast of mind, wit, talent. Not the picturing faculty.

  • imāginātiō, imāginātiōnis f. — a fancy, a mental picture

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Tac. Ann. 15.36: prōvinciās sēcrētīs imāginātiōnibus agitāns (Lewis & Short); Plin. NH 20.68; M-O s.v. imagination: a mental picture

    (post-Augustan: Plin., Tac.)

    A thing imagined, a fancy, rather than the faculty; Augustine uses it more freely (Conf. 7.5).

  • phantasia, phantasiae f. — a fancy, a notion

    noun, first declension · also used · post-classical · Sen. Suas. 2.15 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. imagination

    Greek; Cicero writes it in Greek and translates it vīsum (Lewis & Short). Petronius’s phantasia, nōn homō (38) is a mere figment of a man.

Examples

  • fingite animīs — līberae sunt enim nostrae cōgitātiōnēs et quae volunt sīc intuentur ut ea cernimus quae vidēmus

    imagine it — for our thoughts are free, and they see what they wish as plainly as we see what is before our eyesCic. Mil. 79

See also imagine.

SourcesLewis & Short: cogitatio · Lewis & Short: ingenium · Lewis & Short: imaginatio · Lewis & Short: phantasia
